faqs.question: What is dividend yield?
faqs.answer: Dividend yield is the annual dividend per share divided by the stock price, expressed as a percentage. For example, a $50 stock paying a $2 annual dividend has a 4% yield (2 ÷ 50 × 100).

faqs.question: How does dividend reinvestment work?
faqs.answer: A DRIP (Dividend Reinvestment Plan) automatically uses your dividends to buy more shares, usually commission-free. This accelerates growth through compounding - your dividends buy more shares, which then generate more dividends.

faqs.question: How are dividends taxed?
faqs.answer: Qualified dividends are taxed at the lower long-term capital gains rates (0%, 15%, or 20%). Non-qualified dividends are taxed at your ordinary income rate. The stock must be held for more than 60 days during the ex-dividend period to qualify for qualified treatment.

faqs.question: Is a higher dividend yield always better?
faqs.answer: No. Unusually high yields (>8%) may signal a falling stock price or unsustainable dividends. Sustainable yields typically fall in the 2-6% range. Check the payout ratio - dividends paying out more than 60-70% of earnings may be at risk.

faqs.question: How are calories burned calculated?
faqs.answer: Calories burned are estimated using MET (Metabolic Equivalent of Task) values, which represent the energy cost of an activity. The formula is: Calories = MET × weight (kg) × time (hours).

faqs.question: Which activities burn the most calories?
faqs.answer: High-intensity activities such as running, jump rope, and HIIT burn the most calories per minute. However, the best activity is one you can sustain consistently.

faqs.question: Are calorie burn estimates accurate?
faqs.answer: These are estimates based on average MET values. Individual variation exists due to differences in fitness level, efficiency, and body composition. Use these numbers to track trends rather than absolute accuracy.

metadata.title: FIRE Calculator
metadata.description: Calculate your Financial Independence number and years needed for early retirement.

faqs.question: What is the FIRE movement?
faqs.answer: FIRE (Financial Independence, Retire Early) is a movement focused on retiring before the traditional retirement age through aggressive saving and investing. A typical goal is accumulating 25 times your annual expenses in net worth.

faqs.question: What is the 4% rule?
faqs.answer: The 4% rule suggests you can withdraw 4% of your portfolio in the first year of retirement, then adjust that amount for inflation each year, with a very low probability of running out of money. 25 times your annual expenses achieves this.

faqs.question: How much do I need to FIRE?
faqs.answer: Multiply your annual expenses by 25. If you spend $40,000 per year, you need $1 million (40,000 × 25). This assumes a 4% safe withdrawal rate based on historical market returns.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Lean FIRE and Fat FIRE?
faqs.answer: Lean FIRE targets minimal expenses (typically under $40,000 per year), requiring less savings but a tighter budget. Fat FIRE targets luxurious spending (over $100,000 per year), requiring a larger portfolio ($2.5 million+).

metadata.title: VAT Calculator

faqs.question: What is VAT?
faqs.answer: VAT (Value Added Tax) is a consumption tax levied on the value added to goods or services at each stage of the supply chain. It is ultimately borne by the end consumer, and businesses remit it to the government.

faqs.question: How do I calculate the gross price from a net price?
faqs.answer: Gross price = Net price × (1 + VAT rate). If the net price is $100 and VAT is 20%: gross price = 100 × 1.20 = $120.

faqs.question: How do I extract the net price from a gross price?
faqs.answer: Net price = Gross price ÷ (1 + VAT rate). If the gross price is $120 and VAT is 20%: net price = 120 ÷ 1.20 = $100.

faqs.question: What is the difference between VAT and GST?
faqs.answer: GST (Goods and Services Tax) is a single-stage tax collected at the point of final sale. VAT is a multi-stage tax collected at each stage of the supply chain, with credits along the way. Both function similarly but differ in structure.

metadata.title: Break Even Calculator
metadata.description: Calculate the break-even point - the number of units needed to cover fixed and variable costs.

faqs.question: What is the break-even point?
faqs.answer: The break-even point is where total revenue equals total costs - no profit and no loss. Above it, the business is profitable; below it, the business loses money.

faqs.question: How do I calculate the break-even point (in units)?
faqs.answer: Break-even units = Fixed costs ÷ (Selling price - Variable cost per unit). If fixed costs are $10,000, the selling price is $50, and variable costs are $30: break-even = 10,000 ÷ (50 - 30) = 500 units.

faqs.question: What is the difference between fixed and variable costs?
faqs.answer: Fixed costs do not change with production levels (rent, insurance, salaries). Variable costs change with production (raw materials, direct labor, shipping). Identifying both is essential for an accurate break-even analysis.

faqs.question: Why is break-even analysis important?
faqs.answer: It tells you how much you need to sell to start making a profit, informing pricing, cost control, and business planning. It helps evaluate the viability of new products or the impact of changes on profitability.

faqs.question: What debt-to-income (DTI) ratios do lenders use?
faqs.answer: Most lenders prefer the 28/36 rule - housing costs at no more than 28% of gross income and total debt (including housing) at no more than 36%. Some loans allow DTI up to 43-50%, but they carry more risk.

faqs.question: Should I budget for home maintenance?
faqs.answer: Yes. The rule of thumb is 1-3% of the home's value per year. A $300,000 home should have $3,000-$9,000 budgeted annually for maintenance - HVAC, roof, plumbing, and more. This is not in the mortgage payment but is essential.

faqs.question: What is the 28/36 rule?
faqs.answer: The 28/36 rule suggests your housing expenses (principal, interest, taxes, insurance) should not exceed 28% of your monthly gross income, and total debt payments (housing + car loans + credit cards, etc.) should not exceed 36%.

faqs.question: How do property taxes and insurance affect affordability?
faqs.answer: They have a significant impact. A $125,000 home pays $1,250 per year in property tax in a 1% state, versus $3,125 in a 2.5% state. This changes what you can afford. Always include taxes and insurance before calculating your home price.

faqs.question: What is APR?
faqs.answer: APR (Annual Percentage Rate) is the true annual cost of a loan expressed as a rate. It includes the interest rate plus fees (origination fees, closing costs, etc.), providing a single comparable number.

faqs.question: What is the difference between APR and the interest rate?
faqs.answer: The interest rate is your cost of borrowing. APR includes the interest rate plus loan fees (origination fees, points, mortgage insurance, closing costs). APR is always equal to or higher than the interest rate and gives the full cost picture.

faqs.question: Why is APR important for comparing loans?
faqs.answer: Lenders may offer a low rate with high fees, or a high rate with low fees. APR combines both into one number, making different loan products from different lenders truly comparable.

faqs.question: Does APR account for early repayment?
faqs.answer: No. APR assumes you hold the loan for its full term. If you pay off early or refinance, the actual cost may be higher because you pay the same fees over a shorter period.

faqs.question: What is the difference between federal and private student loans?
faqs.answer: Federal loans offer income-driven repayment, Public Service Loan Forgiveness, and flexible deferment options. Private loans typically lack these protections but may offer lower rates for borrowers with good credit.

faqs.question: What is income-driven repayment (IDR)?
faqs.answer: IDR plans cap monthly payments at 10-20% of discretionary income depending on the plan. Remaining balances are forgiven after 20-25 years. There are four types: SAVE, PAYE, IBR, and ICR.

faqs.question: Should I refinance my student loans?
faqs.answer: Refinancing private loans with good credit can save on interest, but you lose protections like IDR and PSLF. If you have a stable income and do not seek forgiveness, refinancing may be worthwhile.

faqs.question: How is student loan interest calculated?
faqs.answer: Daily simple interest: daily interest = (outstanding balance × interest rate) ÷ 365. It is then capitalized (added to the principal). Federal loans do not accrue interest during school and grace periods.

faqs.question: What is the difference between short-term and long-term capital gains?
faqs.answer: Short-term gains apply to assets held for less than a year and are taxed at ordinary income rates (10-37%). Long-term gains apply to assets held for more than a year and are taxed at lower rates (0%, 15%, or 20%).

faqs.question: What is the Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT)?
faqs.answer: NIIT is an additional 3.8% tax on investment income for high earners (over $200,000 single, $250,000 married filing jointly). It is added on top of regular capital gains tax.

faqs.question: How do capital gains interact with my other income?
faqs.answer: Capital gains stack on top of your ordinary income. If your total income pushes you into a higher bracket, your gains may face a higher rate. Long-term gains have their own brackets, which may differ from ordinary income.

faqs.question: Can I offset gains with capital losses?
faqs.answer: Yes. Capital losses first offset gains of the same type (short-term against short-term, long-term against long-term). Net losses can offset up to $3,000 of ordinary income. Excess losses carry forward to future years.

faqs.question: How is GPA calculated?
faqs.answer: GPA = total quality points ÷ total credits. Quality points = credits × grade points for each course. A = 4.0, B = 3.0, C = 2.0, D = 1.0, F = 0. Plus/minus adjustments: A- = 3.7, B+ = 3.3, and so on.

faqs.question: What is the difference between weighted and unweighted GPA?
faqs.answer: Unweighted GPA measures all courses on a 4.0 scale. Weighted GPA assigns higher values (typically a 5.0 scale) to honors, AP, or IB courses, recognizing course difficulty. Colleges may use either or both in admissions.

faqs.question: What is a good GPA?
faqs.answer: An unweighted 3.0-3.4 is considered good, while 3.5+ is very competitive. Weighted GPA varies by school profile. Top universities typically expect weighted GPAs above 4.0 (due to honors courses).

faqs.question: How can I improve my GPA?
faqs.answer: Focus on high-scoring courses to raise your cumulative GPA. Retake low-grade courses (if allowed). Balance challenging courses with ones you can do well in. Discuss strategies with your advisor.

metadata.title: Grade Calculator

faqs.question: How do I calculate my class grade?
faqs.answer: Multiply each category's score by its weight, then add them up. For example: Tests (50%) = 85 × 0.50 = 42.5, Homework (30%) = 90 × 0.30 = 27, Quizzes (20%) = 80 × 0.20 = 16. Total = 85.5%.

faqs.question: What score do I need to get an A?
faqs.answer: Subtract your current weighted total from the grade you want (90% for an A), then divide by the weight of the remaining category. If you have 80% and the final is worth 20%: (90 - 80) ÷ 0.20 = 50%. You need to score 50% on the final.

faqs.question: What is the difference between weighted and unweighted grades?
faqs.answer: Weighted grades account for the percentage value of each assignment and category weights. Unweighted is simply the total score divided by the total possible. Weighted is more accurate because different assignments have different importance.

faqs.question: How does dropping the lowest score affect my grade?
faqs.answer: Dropping the lowest score usually raises your grade, especially if it is significantly below your average. It works by removing the outlier that drags your average down. Calculate with and without the drop to see the difference.

faqs.answer: These numbers use JavaScript's Math.random(), which is a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG). It is suitable for games, simulations, and general purposes. For cryptographic use, try our password generator, which uses the Web Crypto API.

faqs.answer: Yes! Uncheck 'Allow repeats' to generate numbers without repetition. This uses the Fisher-Yates shuffle algorithm for unbiased selection. When repeats are disabled, the count is capped at the range size.

faqs.answer: JavaScript can safely handle integers up to 9,007,199,254,740,991. In practice, any range within ±1 billion works perfectly.

metadata.title: Whois Lookup
metadata.description: Free whois lookup for registrar, creation/expiry dates, status and DNS servers

faqs.question: What is Whois?
faqs.answer: Whois is the protocol for looking up domain registration data. This tool uses its modern standard, RDAP, to return the registrar, creation/expiry dates, domain status and DNS servers.

faqs.question: Why can't I see the registrant's name and email?
faqs.answer: Since the GDPR took effect in 2018, most registrars redact the registrant contact details of personal domains. Only the registrar, dates, status and DNS servers remain public.

faqs.question: Which TLDs are supported?
faqs.answer: Via the rdap.org bootstrap service, most gTLDs (.com, .net, .org, .io and more) and many ccTLDs (.cn, .jp, .de, .uk and more) are supported. A few TLDs without RDAP may return partial data.

faqs.question: How fresh is the data?
faqs.answer: RDAP queries each registry's authoritative data source directly, returning real-time (or registry-cached) information.

faqs.question: Is it free and safe?
faqs.answer: Completely free. Your browser queries the public RDAP service directly; domain registration data is public information, with no sign-up or API key required.

intro.title: What is a Whois lookup?
paragraphs: A domain Whois lookup is a free tool for viewing a domain's public registration data: registrar, creation and expiry dates, domain status, DNS servers and more. It uses RDAP (Registration Data Access Protocol) — the modern standard replacing Whois — to fetch authoritative data directly from each registry.

sections.title: How to use
paragraphs: Enter a domain (e.g. example.com) in the input box and click Look up. The tool automatically strips http://, www. prefixes and lowercases it.
Results are shown field by field: domain, status, created/updated dates, expiry, DNSSEC, registrar, registrant and DNS servers. Click the copy button next to any field to copy it.

sections.title: About RDAP
paragraphs: RDAP is the structured JSON replacement for Whois, mandated by ICANN since 2018. This tool routes to the correct registry's RDAP server via the rdap.org bootstrap service.

faqs.question: What is an IP address lookup?
faqs.answer: An IP address lookup uses RDAP (Registration Data Access Protocol) to view the network an IP belongs to: CIDR block, owner, country/region, network type and status.

faqs.question: How do I see my public IP?
faqs.answer: Open the tool and it automatically detects and displays your public IP and its network information. Click Refresh to re-detect.

faqs.question: Does it support IPv6?
faqs.answer: RDAP supports both IPv4 and IPv6. The current input box accepts IPv4 format; IPv6 lookup is being improved.

faqs.question: How accurate are the results?
faqs.answer: Data comes from the official RDAP services of the five Regional Internet Registries (ARIN, RIPE, APNIC, LACNIC, AFRINIC) — authoritative network allocation information.

faqs.question: Is it free and safe?
faqs.answer: Completely free. Your browser queries the public RDAP service directly — no sign-up, no API key.

faqs.question: What is a binary converter?
faqs.answer: A binary converter is a tool that converts numbers between binary (base 2), decimal (base 10), hexadecimal (base 16), and octal (base 8).

faqs.question: How do I convert numbers?
faqs.answer: Enter a number in the input field. Select the base of the number you entered. The tool automatically converts it to all other bases and displays the results.

faqs.question: What is the difference between binary and decimal?
faqs.answer: Binary uses base 2 (only the digits 0 and 1), while decimal uses base 10 (digits 0-9). Binary is used in computing; decimal is used for everyday counting.

faqs.question: What is hexadecimal?
faqs.answer: Hexadecimal is a base 16 number system using digits 0-9 and letters A-F. It is commonly used in computing to represent color codes, memory addresses, and other values.

faqs.question: What is octal?
faqs.answer: Octal is a base 8 number system using digits 0-7. It is sometimes used in computing, particularly for Unix permissions.

faqs.question: Is the converter safe?
faqs.answer: Yes. This tool converts numbers locally in your browser. No data is sent to any server.

metadata.title: Due Date Calculator
metadata.description: Estimate your due date based on your last menstrual period, with pregnancy week tracking and key milestones.

faqs.question: How is the due date calculated?
faqs.answer: Using Naegele's rule: add 280 days (40 weeks) to the first day of your last menstrual period (LMP). This assumes a 28-day cycle - the calculator adjusts for different cycle lengths.

faqs.question: Is the due date calculator accurate?
faqs.answer: Only about 4% of babies are born on their exact due date. Most are born within 2 weeks of it. The due date is an estimate - healthcare providers may adjust it based on ultrasound measurements.

faqs.question: What is the conception date?
faqs.answer: Conception typically occurs about 14 days after the first day of your last period (at ovulation). This adjusts with cycle length - longer cycles mean later ovulation.

metadata.title: Pace Calculator
metadata.description: Calculate running pace, finish time, or distance, with common race presets.

faqs.question: How do I calculate pace?
faqs.answer: Pace = time ÷ distance. If you run 3.1 miles in 25 minutes: 25 ÷ 3.1 = 8:04/mile pace. For kilometers, divide by the distance in kilometers instead.

faqs.question: What is a good running pace?
faqs.answer: It varies widely. Beginners: 10-13 minutes/mile. Intermediate: 8-10 minutes/mile. Advanced: 6-8 minutes/mile. Elite: under 5 minutes/mile. Focus on personal progress, not comparisons.

faqs.question: How do I convert pace to speed?
faqs.answer: Speed (mph) = 60 ÷ pace (minutes per mile). An 8:00/mile pace = 60 ÷ 8 = 7.5 mph. An 8:00/km pace = 7.5 km/h.
